summary: A modular monolith build: React Native on the frontend, Python + Django for the backend, PostgreSQL for data, hosted on DigitalOcean for about $69-488 a month. It keeps data in India under DPDP, builds on the team's Python, keeps working offline, and ships as one deployable that a team of 2 can build in 10 weeks.

frontend.justification: React Native (Expo) is the app for a Mobile-first app project with about 400 daily users (~8.3 requests/s at peak), built by a team of 2 in 10 weeks. It builds the Android app now, and the same code can ship an iOS app later without a rewrite. It leads the runner-up, Flutter, by 3.5 stack points (points of the overall stack score, the average of the four layer scores).

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.5 points. React Native (Expo) is stronger on team skill match (4.5 vs 1.5), learning curve (5.0 vs 3.0); Flutter is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0).
Ruled out: Web-only framework; you target iOS/Android only
Ruled out: Web-only framework; you target iOS/Android only
Ruled out: Web-only framework; you target iOS/Android only

tradeoffs: Heavy animations / complex native integrations need native modules
App-store review cycle still applies to native changes

backend.justification: Python + Django serves the API at about 8.3 requests/s at peak (Small (50-500 users online at once)) for a team of 2. The team lists Python, so it needs no new server language (team skill match 4.5/5). It runs as a long-running Python service, so background jobs and database connection pools live in one deployable process. Python + FastAPI is within 0.5 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); Python + Django has the higher stack score.

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.5 points lower; either is defensible. Python + Django is stronger on ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 4.0), structure for large teams (4.0 vs 2.0); Python + FastAPI is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 2.7 points. Python + Django is stronger on development speed (5.0 vs 4.0), structure for large teams (4.0 vs 1.0); Node.js + Express is stronger on hiring pool (5.0 vs 4.0), realtime fit (4.0 vs 2.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 10.7 points. Python + Django is stronger on team skill match (4.5 vs 1.5), learning curve (5.0 vs 2.0); Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), scalability (5.0 vs 4.0); Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot takes a penalty: Nobody on the team listed Java/Kotlin or a closely related skill: a new server language to learn. 1.0 of the 10.7 points come from a stack compatibility rule: Git-push deploys with managed database add-ons are the shortest path to production for a monolith.
Ruled out: Only for read-only sites; your users sign in, post or pay

tradeoffs: Sync-first ORM; async support is partial

database.justification: Your data is mainly relational and reaches about 100 GB within 12 months; PostgreSQL fits relational data 5/5. Strong consistency is assumed, since no input says stale reads are acceptable, and PostgreSQL gives it: a read after a write always sees that write. The workload is write-heavy, and its write scaling scores 3/5. Its share of the estimated bill is $50-$400 a month, against a total budget of $100 a month. It leads the runner-up, MySQL, by 1.0 stack points.

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 1.0 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on cost at your scale (3.8 vs 2.8), realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 6.1 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on data-model fit (4.4 vs 2.6), cost at your scale (3.8 vs 2.6); MongoDB is stronger on team skill match (3.5 vs 1.5), offline support (2.0 vs 1.0); MongoDB takes a penalty: Minimum ~$60/month uses most of the budget.
Ruled out: Eventually consistent; cannot be the system of record for ACID data; In-memory store: ~100 GB within 12 months cannot sensibly live in RAM as the system of record (use it as a cache)
Ruled out: Eventually consistent; cannot be the system of record for ACID data

tradeoffs: Single-writer primary: write scale-out needs sharding (Citus) or Aurora Limitless
Connection-per-process model needs PgBouncer/RDS Proxy under serverless

hosting.choice: DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs), region BLR1 (Bangalore)
hosting.justification: DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) hosts the stack for users in India at a 99% availability target. It runs the Python + Django API as long-running processes, sized for ~8.3 requests/s at peak. It has a region in India, so data can stay in the country. Its share of the estimated bill is $12-$50 a month, against a total budget of $100 a month. Google Cloud Run is within 0.6 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) has the higher stack score.

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.6 points lower; either is defensible. DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) is stronger on realtime fit (4.0 vs 3.0); Google Cloud Run is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), scalability (5.0 vs 4.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 7.6 points. DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) is stronger on portability (low lock-in) (4.0 vs 3.0), realtime fit (4.0 vs 2.0); Vercel is stronger on learning curve (5.0 vs 4.0), performance / latency (5.0 vs 3.0). A stack compatibility rule costs it 9.0 points, more than the whole gap, while on this layer's own criteria it is 1.4 points ahead: Frontend platforms run code only as short-lived functions; this framework expects a long-running server. Ruled out: No India region; data must stay in India

supporting.justification: Send emails, process uploads and call slow APIs outside the request path. Celery with a Redis broker (or RQ / Dramatiq) keeps its jobs in Redis, so the app needs a Redis/Valkey instance (DigitalOcean Managed Caching (Valkey)).

supporting.choice: S3-compatible storage in an Indian region (Amazon S3 Mumbai or Google Cloud Storage asia-south1) + CDN
supporting.justification: Uploaded files and video belong in object storage, not the database.

supporting.choice: CDN in front of the object storage, with image resizing at the edge
supporting.justification: Serve uploads from the CDN, not the app server; resize images on the fly instead of storing every size.

supporting.choice: MSG91 or Twilio Verify, with DLT-registered SMS templates
supporting.justification: One-time codes need an SMS gateway with rate limits against SMS-pumping fraud; Indian operators deliver only DLT-registered templates.

supporting.choice: Keycloak self-hosted in your Indian region, or framework built-in auth
supporting.justification: Do not hand-roll password storage, MFA or SSO.

supporting.choice: PowerSync or ElectricSQL: a local SQLite copy on the device kept in sync with Postgres
supporting.justification: Offline use needs a local copy of the data and conflict handling when the device reconnects; the primary database does not provide that by itself.

supporting.choice: Firebase Cloud Messaging (+ APNs) or Expo Notifications
supporting.justification: Standard channel for mobile engagement on Android and iOS.

supporting.choice: OpenTelemetry instrumentation -> the host's built-in metrics and logs, kept in your Indian region; self-hosted Grafana + Prometheus + Loki there once you outgrow them
supporting.justification: Traces, metrics and error tracking from day one; required to defend an availability target.
Every push runs the tests and deploys the same way; hosted runners mean no build server to operate.

alternatives.why_not: Equivalent pipelines; one more tool to learn for no gain here

tradeoffs: Pipeline minutes are metered on hosted runners

Database: PostgreSQL: $50-400 (Medium (100 GB-1 TB of data) database tier (~100 GB in 12 months); priced as DigitalOcean Managed PostgreSQL)

compliance: DPDP Act 2023 (in force through the DPDP Rules 2025, notified November 2025 and phased in over 18 months) allows cross-border transfer except to notified countries, so it adds consent/breach-notice duties but not an India-region filter. Set infrastructure.data_residency to india if a sector rule (e.g. RBI) applies.
